content: Pilosa, please take over this page and consider applying to become the Editor-in-Chief for this topic. It is possible for there to be one or more Editors-in-Chief. Additionally, you may apply to serve as an Associate Editor-in-Chief for one of the subtopics listed below. If you are interested in serving as either the Editor-in-Chief for the entire topic or as an Associate Editor-in-Chief for a specific subtopic, please contact us via email. Be sure to include your CV and/or a biographical sketch with your application. The order Pilosa is a group of placental mammals that are currently found exclusively in the Americas. This order includes anteaters and sloths. The evolutionary origins of Pilosa can be traced back to the early Tertiary period, approximately 60 million years ago, which was shortly after the extinction of the dinosaurs. The presence of these animals in North America is attributed to the Great American Interchange, a significant biogeographical event. Until recently, Pilosa was grouped together with armadillos under the order Xenarthra. However, Xenarthra is now generally recognized as a superorder. Historically, the families within Pilosa were classified alongside pangolins and aardvarks under the order Edentata. The term Edentata means toothless, as members of this group either lack front incisor teeth and molars or possess poorly developed molars. It was later determined that Edentata was a polyphyletic group, meaning it included unrelated families, and as such, the classification was deemed invalid.
